### Goals

By the end of this session, you should be able to:

- Summarize and describe continuous quantitative variables.

- Explain key measures of central tendency: mean, median, and mode.

- Explain measures of variability: quartiles, interquartile range, range, variance, and standard deviation.

- Describe measures of distribution shape: skewness and kurtosis.

- Create clear visualizations of continuous data in R, including:

    - Histograms

    - Density plots

    - Stem-and-leaf displays

    - Boxplots

---

### Introducing the dataset

Imagine you are working for the World Health Organization (WHO), exploring life expectancy across different regions.

Using this dataset, we can ask questions such as:

- How does life expectancy compare between high-income countries and middle- or low-income countries?

- Do populations in countries with more years of schooling tend to live longer, on average?

--

<div id="infobox">

⚠️ <b>Important note</b>: These questions sound causal, but in this exercise we are not establishing causality. Our goal here is purely descriptive and educational.

</div>

--

Before diving into comparisons of socioeconomic conditions or more advanced analysis, it’s essential to begin with a careful description of the variables related to our research question.

--

First look at the dataset:

.tiny[

```{r, echo=TRUE,eval=FALSE,comment='',indent = '         '}
life_exp <- read.table(file   = "./resources/datasets/life_expectancy.csv",
                       sep    = ",",
                       header = TRUE) %>%
    
head(life_exp)
```
]

# Describing Continuous Variables with Distributions

---

### What is a distribution?

> A distribution describes how the values of a variable are spread across possible outcomes, showing how often (frequency) or how likely (probability) each outcome occurs in a set of observations.

To see a distribution in practice, we often begin with a frequency table, which organizes the data by listing each unique value of a variable and the number of times it occurs.

Consider the life expectancy variable from the sample dataset for different countries in the year 2015 (180 observations). For demonstration purposed, I rounded the values to the nearest integer.

.small[
```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,comment='',indent = '  '}
life_exp <- read.table(file   = here("resources/datasets/life_expectancy.csv"),
                         sep    = ",",
                         header = TRUE)

life_exp_2015 <- filter(life_exp,Year==2015)

life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy <- round(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy,0)
  
for(i in seq(1,180,18)){
  cat(paste0(sprintf("%.0f", life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy[i:(i+17)]),collapse=', '),'\n')
}
```
]

---

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,comment='',indent = '         '}
o <- as.matrix(table(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy))
colnames(o) <- c('Frequency')
v <- as.numeric(rownames(o))
o <- as.data.frame(o)
o$Value <- v
o <- o[,2:1]

o1 <- o[1:18,]
o2 <- o[19:36,]

rownames(o1) <- NULL
rownames(o2) <- NULL
```

.pull-left[

.tiny[
```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE}
knitr::kable(o1)
```
]
]

.pull-right[

.tiny[
```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE}

```
]
]

---
### Histogram

We can graph this frequency table using a plot called **histogram**. Each bar in this histogram is called a **bin**. 

In this plot, I visualized each unique value as a separate bin. This is equivalent to the frequency table, but displayed visually.

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=5}

hist(x      = life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy,
     breaks = 50:89,
     col    = 'white',
     xlab   = 'Life Expectancy',
     main   = '')

```

---

- When data are spread across many unique values, a histogram with one bin per value may look sparse and hard to interpret. 

- We can collapse bins into wider intervals (e.g., 5 years) to make the histogram more compact and reveal the overall distribution pattern more clearly.

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=5}

hist(x      = life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy,
     breaks = seq(50, 90, 5),
     col    = 'white',
     xlab   = 'Life Expectancy',
     main   = '')
```

---

### Stem-and-leaf plot
  
> A stem-and-leaf plot is a way to display the distribution of a continuous variable while preserving the actual data values.

- The stem represents the leading digits (e.g., tens).

- The leaf represents the final digit (e.g., ones).

- Each row groups observations with the same stem, showing the spread of values within that group.

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=5, comment=""}
stem(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy,scale=0.5)
```

This plot is similar to a histogram but keeps the original data values visible, making it useful for small to moderately sized datasets.

---

### Density

> A density plot can be thought of as a smoothed version of a histogram, showing the overall shape of a distribution.

- Instead of discrete bins, the density curve is continuous.

- The y-axis values represent the probability density function (PDF).

    - You don’t need to calculate these values — just understand they describe the likelihood of different values.

- The area under the curve = 1, so it represents the whole distribution.

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=4, comment=""}
d <- density(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy)

plot(d,
     main = "Density Plot of Life Expectancy (2015)",
     xlab = "Life Expectancy",
     ylab = "Density")
```

---

Higher peaks correspond to more common values of life expectancy. 

Any point on the curve reflects the relative likelihood of observing that value if we drew one observation at random.

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=6, comment=""}
d <- density(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy)

plot(d,
     main = "Density Plot of Life Expectancy (2015)",
     xlab = "Life Expectancy",
     ylab = "Density")
```

---
class: middle, inverse
# Describing Continuous Variables with Summary Statistics

---

### Measures of Central Tendency

- Central tendency measures describe the center of a distribution.

- The three most common statistics are:

    - Mean

    - Median

    - Mode

- These measures differ in how much of the data they use:

    - The mode uses the least information (only the most frequent value).

    - The mean uses the most information (every observation).


---

**Mode**

- The mode is the value that occurs most frequently in a dataset

- Simplest measure of central tendency.

- Represents the most common value or “typical” observation.

Example data:

> 8, 9, 8, 7, 10, 9, 6, 4, 9, 8, 7, 8, 10, 9, 8, 6, 9, 7, 8, 8

What is the mode of this data?

Sort the data first.

> 4, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 10, 10

- The most frequent value is 8 → mode = 8.

- We can say the data is “centered” around 8.

---

**Mode**
  
Sometimes there may be more than one mode.
  
  > 4, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, **8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9,** 10, 10

- Both 8 and 9 appear seven times.

- We would report both.

The mode, as a single statistic, is rarely used in practice because it can be unstable and overly sensitive to small data quirks.

In our sample dataset, the mode life expectancy is 75 and 76.

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=4, comment=""}
d <- density(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy)

plot(d,
     main = "Density Plot of Life Expectancy (2015)",
     xlab = "Life Expectancy",
     ylab = "Density")

abline(v = 75.5,lty=2)

legend("topright",                  
       legend = c("Mode (75)"), 
       lty = c(2),                  
       col = c("black"),
       bty = "n")            
```

---

**Median**

- The median is the midpoint of the data when all observations are ordered from smallest to largest.

- 50% of the observations fall **at or below** the median.

- Also called the *50th percentile of a distribution* of *2nd quartile*.

How to find it:

- Sort the data first

- Compute $(n+1)/2$, where $n$ is the number of observations. This is the **midpoint** 

- If $n$ is odd, the midpoint position is the the median.

- If $n$ is even, take the average of the two values around the midpoint.

---

Example (Odd, $n$=11): 

> 4, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10, 10

  - Midpoint position = (11+1)/2=6

  - The 6th value is 8 → median = 8.

Example (Even, $n$=10): 

> 4, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10

  - Midpoint position = (10+1)/2=5.5.

  - Average of 5th and 6th values = (7+8)/2=7.5.

  - Median = 7.5.
  
---

In our sample dataset, the median life expectancy is 74.

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=6, comment=""}

d <- density(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy)

plot(d,
     main = "Density Plot of Life Expectancy (2015)",
     xlab = "Life Expectancy",
     ylab = "Density")

abline(v = 75.5,lty=2)
abline(v = 74,lty=3)  

legend("topright",    
       legend = c("Mpde (75)", "Median (74)"),  
       lty = c(2, 3),                             
       col = c("black", "black"),
       bty = "n")                 
           
```

---

**Mean**

- The mean (arithmetic average) is the most commonly used measure of central tendency.

- Defined as the sum of all values divided by the number of observations.

$$\bar{x} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i}{N}$$
Example Data:

> 4, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 10, 10

- Number of observations: # $N = 20$

- Sum of all values: # $158$

- Therefore:

$$\bar{x} = \frac{158}{20} = 7.9$$
---

In our sample dataset, the mean life expectancy is 71.75.

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=6, comment=""}

d <- density(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy)

plot(d,
     main = "Density Plot of Life Expectancy (2015)",
     xlab = "Life Expectancy",
     ylab = "Density")

abline(v = 75.5,lty=2)    
abline(v = 74,lty=3)      
abline(v = 71.75,lty=4)   

# Add a legend
legend("topright",                       
       legend = c("Mode (75)", "Median (74)", "Mean (71.75)"),  
       lty = c(2, 3, 4),                         
       col = c("black", "black", "black"),       
       bty = "n")                                
```

---

**Pros and Cons of Central Tendency Measures**

- The choice of central tendency measure depends on how well it represents the variable.

- **Symmetric distribution, no extreme scores** → mean, median, and mode are all close, so the mean is a natural choice.

- **Advantages of the mean:**

    - Can be expressed with a formula and manipulated algebraically.

    - Plays a central role in statistical theory (e.g., Central Limit Theorem).

- **Limitations of the mean:**

    - Highly sensitive to extreme scores (outliers).

    - May misrepresent the “center” in skewed or heavy-tailed distributions.

- Median is more robust to extreme values and may be preferred when extreme values are present.

- Mode is simple but less informative and rarely used alone, though it can describe the overall shape of a distribution.

---

- Humans on Mars and Venus have very low life expectancies (for now).

- Question: How would adding these two (as zeros) change the mode, mean, and median for life expectancy?

.small[
```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,comment='',indent = '  '}

my_vec <- c(round(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy,0),0,0)
  
for(i in seq(1,180,18)){
  cat(paste0(sprintf("%.0f", life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy[i:(i+17)]),collapse=', '),'\n')
}

cat(paste0(c(0,0),collapse=', '))

```
]

|  | Without Extreme Values | With Extreme Values  |
|-------|:------:|:------:|
| Mean    | 71.75  | 70.96   |
| Median  | 74     | 74     |
| Mode    | 75     | 75     |

---

### Comparing distributions

- These distributions have the same central tendency (mean = 100).

- .blue[How are they different?]

```{r, echo = F}
narrow <- tibble(values = rnorm(10000, mean = 100, sd = 5)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(values)) +
  geom_density(adjust = 3, fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  theme_classic() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 100, color = "red") +
  xlim(c(70,130))

wide <- tibble(values = rnorm(10000, mean = 100, sd = 10)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(values)) +
  geom_density(adjust = 3, fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.4) +
  theme_classic() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 100, color = "red") +
  xlim(c(70,130))

narrow2 <- tibble(values = rnorm(10000, mean = 100, sd = 1.5)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(values)) +
  geom_density(adjust = 3, fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  theme_classic() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 100, color = "red") +
  xlim(c(70,130))


gridExtra::grid.arrange(narrow, wide, narrow2, wide, nrow = 2)
```

---

### Measures of Variability

- Central tendency describes the center of a distribution.

- But distributions can share the same mean/median and still look very different.

- We often want to know:

    - How much do values vary across observations?

    - How far does a “typical” observation deviate from the mean?

**Key Measures of Variability:**

- Range (min to max)

- Interquartile Range (IQR) (middle 50% of values)

- Variance (average squared deviation from mean)

- Standard Deviation (SD) (typical distance from mean, in original units)

---

**Range**

- The range is the distance between the minimum and maximum values in a dataset.

- Simple to compute, but only depends on two numbers (can be distorted by extreme values).

$$Range = Max - Min$$
Example Data:

> 62, 64, 66, 70, 72, 76, 77, 81, 81

Min = 62

Max = 81

Range = 81 – 62 = 19

---

**Interquartile Range (IQR)**

The IQR is the difference between the 1st quartile (Q1 = 25th percentile) and the 3rd quartile (Q3 = 75th percentile).

$$IQR = Q_3 - Q_1$$

- The IQR summarizes the middle 50% of the data (the most typical values).

- More robust to outliers than the range, because it ignores the extreme highs and lows.


```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=4, comment=""}

ggplot(life_exp_2015, aes(x = Life.expectancy)) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = quantile(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy, .25)) +
  geom_label(
    x = quantile(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy, .25),
    y = .03,
    label = paste("25th %ile =", quantile(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy, .25))
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = quantile(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy, .75)) +
  geom_label(
    x = quantile(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy, .75),
    y = .03,
    label = paste("75th %ile =", quantile(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy, .75))
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    x = quantile(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy, .25),
    xend = quantile(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy, .75),
    y = .015,
    yend = .015,
    linetype = 2
  ) +
  geom_label(x = 71.5,
             y = 0.01,
             label = "IQR = 11") +
  theme_classic()
  
```

---

**Variance**

- Variance measures the average squared deviation of each observation from the mean.

$$s^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}{N - 1}$$
- We divide by 𝑁−1 instead of N to correct for bias when estimating the population variance from a sample.

---

Breaking down the variance formula:

| observed value | mean | deviance | deviance² |
|:--------------:|:----:|:--------:|:---------:|
|       62       | 72.1 |  -10.1   |  102.01   |
|       64       | 72.1 |  -8.11   |   65.77   |
|       66       | 72.1 |  -6.11   |   37.33   |
|       70       | 72.1 |  -2.11   |    4.45   |
|       72       | 72.1 |  -0.111  |    0.01   |
|       76       | 72.1 |   3.89   |   15.13   |
|       77       | 72.1 |   4.89   |   23.90   |
|       81       | 72.1 |   8.89   |   79.03   |
|       81       | 72.1 |   8.89   |   79.03   |
| **Σ**          |      | **0**    | **406.66**|

$$s^2 = \frac{406.66}{9-1}=50.83$$
---

**Standard Deviation (SD)**

- Variance is useful but expressed in squared units, which makes it less intuitive.

- To bring variability back into the original units of measurement, we take the square root of the variance.

- This gives us the standard deviation (SD) — the most commonly reported measure of spread.

$$s = \sqrt{s^2}$$


- Standard deviation represents the typical distance of observations from the mean.

- Larger SD → data are more spread out.

- Smaller SD → data are more tightly clustered around the mean.

---

**Statistical Notation**

Statistics usually have two notational forms:

- Population statistics (Greek letters) → describe the full universe of possible values.

- Sample statistics (Roman letters) → describe actual values in our data.

.pull-left[
Sample Statistics (Roman Alphabet)

- Mean: $\bar{x}$

- Standard Deviation: $s$

- Variance: $s^2$
]

.pull-right[
Population Statistics (Greek Alphabet)

- Mean: $\mu$

- Standard Deviation: $\sigma$

- Variance: $\sigma^2$
]

---

In practice, we usually use sample statistics to *estimate* population statistics.

An estimated value is denoted with a “hat” symbol.

.pull-left[
Sample Statistics → Population Estimates

- $\bar{x} \rightarrow \hat{\mu}$

- $s \rightarrow \hat{\sigma}$

- $s^2 \rightarrow \hat{\sigma}^2$
]

.pull-right[
Population (Greek Alphabet)

- Mean: $\mu$

- Standard Deviation: $\sigma$

- Variance: $\sigma^2$
]


Greek vs. Roman letters are conventions, not rules.

For example, we could use $\psi$ for the mean — but standard symbols ($\mu$, $\sigma$) reduce cognitive load.

You’ll want to get familiar with the most commonly used notations in textbooks and academic literature.

---

### Measures of Shape

So far, we’ve described a distribution with:

  - Center → mean, median, mode

  - Spread → range, IQR, variance, standard deviation

--

But two distributions can have the same center and spread yet still look very different.

To fully describe a distribution, we also need to consider its shape.

- Skewness → direction and degree of asymmetry

- Kurtosis → “peakedness”, "pointiness", or heaviness of tails

---

**Skewness**

- Not all real-world distributions are symmetrical.

- Many show asymmetry, called **skewness**.

- Skewness describes whether values are “bunched up” more on one side of the mean.

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=4, comment=""}

set.seed(1000)
N <- 10000
x <- tibble(
  pos_skew = rbeta(N, 1.5 ,5),
  neg_skew = rbeta(N, 5, 1.5),
  central  = rbeta(N, 5 , 5)
)

pos_skew <- ggplot(x, aes(pos_skew)) +
  geom_density(adjust = 4, fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  xlim(0, 1) + ylim(0, 2.5) +
  ggtitle("Positive Skew") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank())

neg_skew <- ggplot(x, aes(neg_skew)) +
  geom_density(adjust = 4, fill = "orange", alpha = 0.4) +
  xlim(0, 1) + ylim(0, 2.5) +
  ggtitle("Negative Skew") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank())

normal <- ggplot(x, aes(central)) +
  geom_density(adjust = 2, fill = "gray70", alpha = 0.4) +
  xlim(0, 1) + ylim(0, 2.5) +
  ggtitle("No Skew") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank())

gridExtra::grid.arrange(pos_skew, normal, neg_skew, nrow = 1)

```

---

**Kurtosis**

- *Kurtosis* describes how much values concentrate around the center → the “peakedness” of a distribution.

Types of kurtosis:

- Leptokurtic → more values near the center, taller/narrower peak, heavier tails.

- Mesokurtic  → normal distribution as a reference (no excess kurtosis).

- Platykurtic] → flatter peak, lighter tails, more spread out.

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=4, comment=""}

# Fleischmann coefficients
a <- 0; b <- 0.7373813; c <- 0; d <- 0.08092509   # Kurtosis = 4
e <- 0; f <- 1.221009; g <- 0; h <- -0.08015816   # Kurtosis = -1

set.seed(123)
k <- tibble(central = rnorm(10000, 0, 1)) %>% 
  mutate(
    lepto = a + b*central + c*(central^2) + d*(central^3),
    platy = e + f*central + g*(central^2) + h*(central^3)
  )

# Common plotting function
make_plot <- function(data, var, title, fill_col){
  ggplot(data, aes(.data[[var]])) +
    geom_density(adjust = 4, fill = fill_col, alpha = 0.5) +
    xlim(-3, 3) + ylim(0, 0.5) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(axis.title = element_blank()) +
    ggtitle(title)
}

platy   <- make_plot(k, "platy", "Platykurtic (Flat)", "orange")
central <- make_plot(k, "central", "Mesokurtic (Normal)", "gray70")
lepto   <- make_plot(k, "lepto", "Leptokurtic (Peaked)", "skyblue")

gridExtra::grid.arrange(platy, central, lepto, nrow = 1)


```

---

**Evaluating Skew and Kurtosis**

These can be assessed both visually and quantitatively.

- Skewness

  - Positive skew → Skewness > 0

  - Negative skew → Skewness < 0

- Kurtosis (Excess)

  - Leptokurtic (tall/narrow, heavy tails) → Kurtosis > 0

  - Platykurtic (flat, light tails) → Kurtosis < 0
  
---

**Moments of a Distribution**

Each statistic we’ve introduced corresponds to a different moment (mathematical characteristic) of a distribution:

- Mean (1st moment, location)

$$\mu = \frac{\Sigma(x_i)}{N}$$

- Variance (2nd moment, spread)

$$\sigma^2 = \frac{\Sigma(X_i-\mu)^2}{N}$$

- Skewness (3rd moment, asymmetry)

$$skewness(X) = \frac{1}{N\sigma^3}\Sigma(X_i-\mu)^3$$

- Kurtosis (4th moment, “peakedness” / tails)

$$kurtosis(X) = \frac{1}{N\sigma^4}\Sigma(X_i-\mu)^4 - 3$$

You don’t need to compute these by hand, but you should understand how to interpret them.

---

**Kurtosis: Two Conventions**

- Different software/packages use different definitions of kurtosis.

- This can cause confusion, but the two are directly related.

**Raw Kurtosis (a.k.a. 4th standardized moment)*

$$\frac{1}{N} \sum \left(\frac{X_i - \mu}{\sigma}\right)^4$$
For a normal distribution, raw kurtosis is equal to 3. So, values lower than 3 are platykurtic, and values higher than 3 are leptokurtic.

**Excess Kurtosis**

$$\frac{1}{N} \sum \left(\frac{X_i - \mu}{\sigma}\right)^4 - 3$$

For a normal distribution, excess kurtosis is equal to 0. So, values lower than 0 are platykurtic, and values higher than 0 are leptokurtic.

---

- It is critical that you know which definition of kurtosis is used by any software you use before you interpret the kurtosis value.

In R:

- `moments::kurtosis()` function uses the definition of raw kurtosis


- `psych::describe()` function uses the definition of excess kurtosis

💡 Rule of thumb: When reporting, always state which convention you’re using (raw or excess).

---

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=5, comment=""}

d <- density(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy)

plot(d,
     main = "Density Plot of Life Expectancy (2015)",
     xlab = "Life Expectancy",
     ylab = "Density")
```

Shape: Does the distribution look symmetric or asymmetric?

Skewness: Is there evidence of strong right or left skew?

Kurtosis: Does the curve appear flatter (platykurtic) or more peaked (leptokurtic) compared to a normal distribution?

---

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=5, comment=""}

d <- density(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy)

plot(d,
     main = "Density Plot of Life Expectancy (2015)",
     xlab = "Life Expectancy",
     ylab = "Density")
```

**Numerical Assessment**

- Skewness = -0.50

- Raw Kurtosis = 2.56 (Normal Distribution = 3)

- Excess Kurtosis = -0.44 (Normal Distribution = 0)

The distribution of life expectancy is nearly symmetric, with only mild left skew and slightly flatter peak/tails than a normal curve.


**Narrative Write-up Example**

> The average life expectancy in 2015 ranged from 51 to 88, *M* = 71.75, *SD* = 8.08.

---

**Box-and-whisker plots**

A box-and-whisker plot summarizes a distribution using the five-number summary:

- Min, Q1, Median (Q2), Q3, Max.

- The whiskers extend to the most extreme values within the fences:

Lower fence = Q1 − 1.5·IQR

Upper fence = Q3 + 1.5·IQR

Points outside the fences are shown as extreme values.

(Note: the fences are not part of the five-number summary; they’re a rule to flag outliers.)

---

```{r, echo=FALSE,eval=TRUE,fig.height=9, fig.width=6, comment=""}

# Base boxplot
boxplot(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy,
        col = "orange",
        horizontal = FALSE,
        main = "",
        ylab = "Life Expectancy")

# Add text labels
stats <- boxplot.stats(life_exp_2015$Life.expectancy)$stats

# Components: [lower whisker, Q1, median, Q3, upper whisker]
text(x = 1.25, y = stats[1], labels = "Lower adjacent value", pos = 4, col = "darkgreen")
text(x = 1.25, y = stats[2], labels = "Q1", pos = 4, col = "blue")
text(x = 1.25, y = stats[3], labels = "Median (Q2)", pos = 4, col = "black")
text(x = 1.25, y = stats[4], labels = "Q3", pos = 4, col = "blue")
text(x = 1.25, y = stats[5], labels = "Upper adjacent value", pos = 4, col = "darkgreen")


```

---

```{r, echo = F, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6}

p <- ggplot() +
  geom_density(data=life_exp_2015, 
               aes(x=Life.expectancy),
               alpha=.3) +
  theme(axis.title.y=element_blank(), 
        axis.text.y=element_blank()) +
  xlim(40,100)

dpb <- ggplot_build(p)

q1 <- min(which(dpb$data[[1]]$x >= 66))
q3 <- max(which(dpb$data[[1]]$x <= 77))
lf <- min(which(dpb$data[[1]]$x >= 51))
uf <- max(which(dpb$data[[1]]$x <= 88))


line_label <- function(xint, yint, lbl, clr) {
  list(
    geom_segment(aes(x = xint, xend = xint, y = 0, yend = .1), color = clr, linetype = 2),
    geom_label(aes(x = xint, y = yint), label = lbl, color = clr)
  )
}

p +
  geom_area(data=data.frame(x=dpb$data[[1]]$x[q1:q3],
                            y=dpb$data[[1]]$y[q1:q3]),
            aes(x=x, y=y), fill="purple", alpha = .5) +
  geom_area(data=data.frame(x=dpb$data[[1]]$x[lf:q1],
                            y=dpb$data[[1]]$y[lf:q1]),
            aes(x=x, y=y), fill="cornflowerblue", alpha = .5) +
  geom_area(data=data.frame(x=dpb$data[[1]]$x[q3:uf],
                            y=dpb$data[[1]]$y[q3:uf]),
            aes(x=x, y=y), fill="cornflowerblue", alpha = .5) +
  geom_boxplot(data=life_exp_2015, 
               aes(x=Life.expectancy, y = 0.1),
               alpha=.5,
               fill = "purple", width = 0.05) +
  line_label(xint = 74, clr = "black", yint = .1, lbl = "Median") +
  line_label(xint = 66, clr = "blue", yint = .085, lbl = "Q1") +
  line_label(xint = 77, clr = "blue", yint = .085, lbl = "Q3") +
  line_label(xint = 51, clr = "forestgreen", yint = .07, lbl = "Q1 - 1.5*IQR") +
  line_label(xint = 88, clr = "forestgreen", yint = .07, lbl = "Q3 + 1.5*IQR") +
  theme_minimal()

```
